stories.headline: More Than 60 Christians Killed in Attacks in Ethiopia's Oromia Region, Church Says
stories.summary:
More than 60 people have been killed in a series of attacks on Christians in Ethiopia's Oromia region, according to the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church. The church described the assaults on three areas of the Shirka district as a "massacre" and said 20 houses were burned to the ground. Eyewitnesses told BBC Amharic that five of the dead were children, and many residents have fled the area.

One resident, whose 75-year-old father was killed, described an ambush, saying attackers surrounded the community from all four directions and that villagers had no warning. A church official said security forces arrived at the scene but were unable to stop the assault. The Orthodox Church said attacks on Christians have been increasing and that it has repeatedly raised insecurity concerns with authorities without result.

A local official blamed a newly formed rebel coalition, the Alliance for Survival, which includes the Oromo Liberation Army. The OLA has not commented on this attack and has denied responsibility for earlier ones. The regional government said it would take action against those responsible, and Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has previously said violence targeting civilians and religious institutions is part of a plan to destabilize the country.

The Ethiopian Human Rights Council reported in July that 458 people had been killed in attacks in the area over the previous four years, making this one of the deadliest incidents in that period. Reports have also documented attacks on Muslims in the region, and residents describe the violence as both ethnic and religious. About two-thirds of Ethiopians are Christian, mostly Orthodox, and one third are Muslim.

stories.headline: Vance Attacks Montana Democrats as Midterm Campaigning Intensifies a Week Before Election
stories.summary:
Vice President JD Vance accused Montana Democrats on Monday of hiding behind moderate branding while backing sanctuary city policies, sales taxes and diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives. Speaking at a campaign stop in Belgrade, Montana, he tried to tie state candidates to national party leaders including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and Rep. Nancy Pelosi, warning that any elected Democrat would "bend the knee" to Washington interests.

Vance said congressional Democrats "do not believe in the United States of America" and charged that they have taught young people to be ashamed of the country's history and flag. He singled out Democratic House candidate Sam Forstag over his support for sanctuary cities, a state sales tax and gender transitions for minors, and dismissed claims that state Democrats offer an independent voice.

The event was part of a broader day of midterm news covered by about 20 outlets. President Trump continued his attacks on Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, and the Justice Department defended its lawsuit over the Alaska Senate result. Democrats and their allies have framed the Republican messaging as divisive and as a distraction from economic concerns, while Republicans argue Democratic candidates are out of step with voters on immigration, taxes and cultural issues.

Control of Congress will be decided in the Nov. 3 midterm elections, which are now about a week away. Both parties are stepping up appearances in contested states as early voting continues.

stories.headline: Two Catholic Bishops Apologize for Trump Oval Office Meeting, Saying It Was Exploited
stories.summary:
Two U.S. Catholic bishops have said they regret meeting President Trump at the White House after images of them praying with him circulated widely. Photos and video from the Oct. 22 meeting show bishops standing around Trump at the Resolute Desk, prompting questions about whether they were making a political statement less than two weeks before the midterm elections.

Milwaukee Archbishop Jeffrey Grob said he believed the meeting was private and not "a political photo opportunity." He said the group had held 90 minutes of meetings with officials before being ushered into the Oval Office to pray, and that none of the participants authorized the release of the images. He said he received messages from congregants worried he had joined a political event, and from some who felt wounded by the president's policies.

Bishop William Joensen of Des Moines said the White House Faith Office arranged the meeting to discuss immigration, visas for international clergy and the "exploitation of vulnerable poor persons." He said no one intended to endorse any party or candidate, adding that he wished he had been "more shrewd and less simple, like those who exploited our meeting for partisan political purposes." The video was released by presidential aide Margo Martin. The White House did not address the bishops' remarks directly, with spokeswoman Taylor Rogers saying there has "never been a greater president for Catholic Americans."

The episode comes amid a contentious relationship between Trump and Pope Leo XIV, and as some U.S. bishops have criticized administration immigration policy. Trump won 55% of Catholic voters in 2024, but Pew found his approval among Catholics at 30% this month, down from 47% in 2025.

stories.headline: US Marine Indicted for Murder and Robbery of Woman in Okinawa, Japan
stories.summary:
A U.S. Marine has been indicted over the killing and robbery of a woman in Okinawa, Japan, according to Japanese media reports. Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, stationed at Marine Corps Air Station Futenma, is accused of strangling 39-year-old Anna Yagi with a telephone cord at a hotel in Naha on Oct. 3 and stealing her backpack and wallet.

Security footage allegedly shows a man believed to be the suspect entering the hotel with the woman and leaving alone with her belongings. Reports said Ballard denied the allegations, though Asahi Shimbun and Kyodo News cited investigators saying he made some statements suggesting involvement. The Marine Corps has said it is cooperating with Japanese authorities.

Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi called the crime "brutal and heinous" and said Japan registered a strong protest with the United States, calling for strict discipline and measures to prevent recurrence. Okinawa Governor Genta Koja said the prefecture has repeatedly demanded action and sees the case as a sign of a lack of discipline. About 100 people protested in Naha and Tokyo earlier this month.

Okinawa hosts the highest concentration of the roughly 55,000 U.S. troops in Japan, and crimes by service members have long inflamed local opinion. The largest protests followed a 1995 rape case involving a 12-year-old girl, and recent cases have included sexual assault convictions in 2024 and 2025.

stories.headline: Update: Lula Wins Fourth Term in Brazil Runoff as Flávio Bolsonaro Refuses to Concede
stories.summary:
Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won a fourth term in Sunday's presidential runoff, taking 51.79% of the vote against right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro. Lula is the first president since the return to civilian rule in 1985 to be elected after losing the first round. Bolsonaro, son of convicted former president Jair Bolsonaro, had won the October 4 first round with 47% to Lula's 45%.

Bolsonaro has so far refused to recognize the result, calling it "inexplicable" and demanding that it be annulled. His camp's challenge centers on Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin's decision to extend voting nationwide by two hours. Some Bolsonaro supporters point out that Zanin once served as Lula's lawyer and allege bias. Both campaigns had requested extensions, citing a lack of buses in São Paulo and Bahia and heavy rain in the south and in São Paulo.

Supreme Electoral Court president Kássio Nunes Marques, who was appointed by Jair Bolsonaro, confirmed Lula's victory and said the extension did not change the outcome. The 4.4 million vote margin makes a legal challenge unlikely to succeed. Lula's campaign gained momentum by boosting turnout after 33 million people abstained in round one, producing the largest drop in abstention between rounds since 1989.

In São Paulo, Lula told supporters his win was a "loss for negativity, lies" and promised to listen most to the Brazilian people. World leaders have congratulated him. He faces a divided country and a Congress packed with Bolsonaro allies. Markets reacted negatively, with the São Paulo stock exchange opening 15% lower and briefly suspending trading.

stories.headline: Microsoft Offers Voluntary Buyouts to 60,000 Employees as It Retools for AI
stories.summary:
Microsoft on Monday announced voluntary buyout offers to about 60,000 employees, more than a quarter of its workforce of roughly 223,000. A memo went to employees in the United States, Canada, the UK and India. Bloomberg first reported that the offers are directed at staff in Xbox, Windows, Copilot and finance divisions.

The memo described the voluntary exits as "a few of the ways we're trying to meet different business needs while continuing to create opportunities for our own people to grow and contribute." Employees have until December 31 to decide, according to CNBC. Chief people officer Amy Coleman wrote, "My promise is to continue to provide clarity, listen and learn and keep improving."

The move follows a spring voluntary retirement offer to long-tenured older employees and the layoff of 9,000 workers last year. Microsoft has been investing heavily in AI infrastructure, reporting an 18% revenue increase this summer driven largely by cloud products. It disclosed $130 billion in new data center leases earlier this year, and chief financial officer Amy Hood said the shift in lease accounting would lead to roughly $175 billion in capital expenditures and finance leases.

The company reports earnings on Wednesday, when investors are likely to look for detail on the cost savings and the pace of AI spending. Microsoft did not immediately respond to a request for comment from the New York Post.

stories.headline: Trump's Board of Peace Hires Former Biden Aide to Lead Congressional Outreach
stories.summary:
President Trump's Board of Peace has appointed Shelley Greenspan, who served as the Biden White House's Jewish community liaison, to lead its outreach to Congress and Washington think tanks. Axios reported the appointment Monday.

The selection is part of an effort to broaden bipartisan support for Trump's Gaza peace plan. Hiring a Democratic-administration alumna signals an attempt to win over lawmakers beyond the president's own party, where the plan's reception has been mixed.

Implementation of the plan is expected to get a renewed push after the midterm elections and the formation of a new Israeli government. Israel votes Tuesday, and the result will shape how the next phase proceeds.

stories.headline: Anthropic Details Planned Nasdaq Listing, Warns of 'Catastrophic or Existential Risks' From AI
stories.summary:
Anthropic, developer of the Claude chatbot, unveiled details of its planned stock market listing in the United States on Monday. The company said it will list on the Nasdaq under the symbol ANT and will be the first fully AI-focused company to go public. Its valuation is expected to exceed that of SpaceX, which held the biggest listing on record at an initial valuation of about $1.8 trillion this summer. Anthropic has not yet disclosed the number of shares, the price range or a listing date.

In its filing, the company reported $16.3 billion in revenue for the first half of the year against losses of more than $80.7 billion. It said it would often make forward investments "that may seem irresponsibly large at first glance," adding that it aims to be "bold but sane." The filing, with about 90 pages of risk factors, warned that advanced AI systems could, if not developed and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight and security, pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity," particularly if misused, replicated, weaponised or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy.

The company was founded five years ago by chief executive Dario Amodei, his sister Daniela Amodei and five others, and announced its intention to go public in June. Rival OpenAI followed, with its listing now expected early next year according to a person familiar with its plans. Both firms have faced cyber-security and other breaches involving AI agents, and current and former staff have warned that the technology is being developed without the ability to protect against future harms.

On the same day, the owners of the rights to Elvis Presley's music sued Anthropic, accusing it of using hundreds of his songs to train Claude. The listing is seen as a test case for investor appetite for the AI industry.

stories.headline: Trump Escalates Attacks on Michigan Senate Candidate Abdul El-Sayed Over Faith and Loyalty
stories.summary:
President Trump intensified his rhetoric against Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed at a Sunday rally, portraying him as a national security threat and questioning his loyalty to the United States. Critics condemned the remarks as anti-Muslim. Trump, who imposed a travel ban on several predominantly Muslim countries in his first term, has increasingly leaned into such rhetoric as the election nears. El-Sayed is locked in a dead heat with Republican Mike Rogers, and the race could help decide control of the Senate.

Republican-aligned outlets have focused on separate controversies surrounding El-Sayed. Fox News, the Washington Free Beacon and the Washington Examiner have highlighted a pro-El-Sayed PAC ad blaming Israel for high grocery prices, which drew accusations of antisemitism. They have also reported on a roundtable he held with a Dearborn editor who has made inflammatory statements about Israel and Hamas, and on his earlier pledge to stay as Wayne County health director. Democrats and many commentators say Trump's remarks go beyond fair criticism and target the candidate's religion.

The flare-up comes eight days before the November 3 midterms, with early voting nearing 30 million ballots. Barack Obama campaigned for El-Sayed on Saturday, and Trump rallied in Michigan on Sunday for Rogers and John James. All 435 House seats and one-third of the Senate are on the ballot, and Democrats need to flip four seats in each chamber to take the majority.

stories.headline: Egypt's Parliament Backs El-Sisi's Offer to Defend Saudi Arabia Amid Houthi Strikes
stories.summary:
Egypt's parliament on Monday authorized President Abdel-Fattah El-Sisi to take the steps necessary to defend Saudi Arabia, as Houthi forces in Yemen continue strikes against the kingdom. Legislators approved military support for Riyadh.

At the same time, Cairo has ruled out strikes on Yemen, signaling that the commitment is defensive in nature. The vote follows a wider regional response to the escalating Houthi attacks, and comes as Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan made a joint visit to Tehran on Monday to try to defuse tensions with Iran.

The Egyptian authorization adds to a growing set of regional security moves, including Algeria's parliament approving troops for Niger earlier this week, and underscores concern over a possible renewed US-Israeli campaign against Iran. Countering Houthi advances is expected to be a major focus for Saudi Arabia and its allies.

stories.headline: Judge Rules Firing of Prosecutor Maurene Comey Was Unlawful, Orders Reinstatement
stories.summary:
A federal judge ruled Monday that the Justice Department unlawfully fired Maurene Comey, a longtime Southern District of New York prosecutor and the daughter of former FBI Director James Comey. U.S. District Judge Jesse Furman rejected the Trump administration's argument that it had constitutional authority to dismiss her, and ordered her reinstated with back pay.

Comey was abruptly fired in July 2025 after a decade as an assistant U.S. attorney. She handled high-profile prosecutions, including those of Jeffrey Epstein and Sean Combs. She sued, saying the dismissal came without notice or explanation and was driven by a vendetta against her father, a prominent Trump critic. The judge wrote that the defendants' argument was contrary to the law.

The administration is expected to weigh an appeal. Supporters of the administration have generally argued that the executive branch has broad authority over personnel at the Justice Department, while critics say the ruling shows the firings were politically motivated. The decision lands as the DOJ faces scrutiny over politically sensitive actions in the final days before the midterm elections.

stories.headline: China's Communist Party opens Fifth Plenum as Xi Jinping signals tighter party discipline
stories.summary:
A four-day closed-door meeting of the Chinese Communist Party's Central Committee opened Monday in Beijing, bringing together around 300 members. State media said the session would pave the way for a "tightening of discipline" within the party's ranks. The location has not been announced, though past plenums have been held at Beijing's Jingxi Hotel.

The gathering gives President Xi Jinping an opportunity to consolidate his grip on power following recent purges. According to a September readout from the 21-member Politburo, the plenum will adopt a decision on "several major issues persistently advancing the comprehensive strict governance of the Party." Analysts read this as a way to ensure obedience and effectiveness among distant party officials.

The purges have been extensive. Allegations of corruption, including "moral corruption," have removed large numbers of senior figures. Experts see the "moral corruption" charge as a means of targeting perceived disloyalty to Xi. The Asia Society Policy Institute has estimated that of 44 military members appointed to the Central Committee in 2022, only two have not been taken down, and the Central Military Commission has also been heavily thinned.

The timing matters because the next Party Congress is a year away, where a new central committee will be appointed and Xi is almost certain to be reappointed, term limits having been abolished. Past plenums have been used to declare Xi "the core" of the party and to elevate "Xi Jinping Thought." A summary of decisions will be published when the session ends Thursday, with a more detailed document to follow.

stories.headline: Update: Nurse killed in attack on health workers responding to Ebola alert in DR Congo
stories.summary:
A nurse was killed and another health worker seriously injured in north-eastern Democratic Republic of Congo while responding to an Ebola alert. According to UN-backed Radio Okapi, the two were attacked by local youths who accused them of contaminating water sources and spreading the virus. The World Health Organization condemned the attack.

WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said health workers "must be able to carry out their duties in safety and dignity." The agency extended condolences to the nurse's family and colleagues and wished the injured worker a swift recovery. The BBC has contacted the Ebola response team for comment on the circumstances.

The outbreak, which began in May, has killed more than 4,800 people and infected nearly 10,000 in DR Congo. Earlier this month Kenya and Nigeria reported their first linked cases. The Nigerian patient, the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat, was flown from Abuja to Switzerland for treatment and is stable and conscious. Authorities are trying to determine where she contracted the virus.

Uganda has banned non-essential travel to and from DR Congo and will quarantine returning citizens for 21 days at their own cost. Only essential travellers such as aid workers, truck drivers and security personnel may cross, subject to health screening. Health Minister Chris Baryomunsi said the measures are meant to keep Uganda free of Ebola.

stories.headline: Democrats lay groundwork to investigate Trump's Russian diesel deal if they win Congress
stories.summary:
Top Democrats expected to hold powerful roles next year are demanding that major banks and ports preserve records tied to any imports of or deals involving Russian diesel, according to an Axios exclusive. The move signals that investigations of President Trump's agreement with Moscow would extend beyond the White House into corporate boardrooms.

Probing the diesel agreement would be a priority if Democrats regain control of one or both chambers of Congress in the November midterms, Axios reported. The preservation demands are a standard first step before formal oversight inquiries, which require a majority to issue subpoenas.

Separately, House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries told MSNOW that Democrats will run Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth "out of town" if they take the majority, and will act to remove him if Trump does not. Republicans have generally defended Hegseth and the administration's Russia policy, and have framed such oversight threats as partisan retribution rather than legitimate inquiry.

The midterms are eight days away, and the outcome will determine whether Democrats gain subpoena power over the administration.

stories.headline: Update: Tallahassee police arrest 15-year-old suspect in shooting near Florida A&M stadium
stories.summary:
Tallahassee police arrested a 15-year-old suspect Sunday night in connection with Saturday's shooting near Florida A&M University's Bragg Memorial Stadium, which injured 12 people, including six juveniles. The youngest victim was 11. Police said an altercation preceded the gunfire.

The teen faces 11 counts of attempted second-degree murder and a count of possession of a firearm by a delinquent, police said. Chief of Police Lawrence Revell said in a Monday statement: "What should have been a weekend of celebration in our community instead became a night of fear and violence for the victims and their families."

Revell added that while the arrest is "a significant step forward," the department's work "is far from over," and said police remain committed to holding those responsible accountable and getting answers for every affected family. The shooting occurred during homecoming week.

stories.headline: Israel Launches Largest Military Drills in Years Ahead of Election as Iran Tensions Rise
stories.summary:
The Israeli military began large-scale domestic exercises on Sunday designed to counter surprise infiltrations and ground raids across northern and central Israel. The drills, scheduled to run 48 hours, involve the Northern Command's 210th Division, the West Bank Division, the Central Command's 98th and 96th divisions, and the Israeli Air Force. The IDF said troops would rehearse scenarios including surprise attacks and infiltration by air and land, drawing on lessons from the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attacks.

The exercises come just before Israel's general election on Oct. 27 and follow an Iranian show of force days earlier, in which the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps reportedly fired roughly 30 ballistic missiles of two weapon classes. That display renewed alerts about commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and led the Israeli military to raise its alert level.

Israeli security analyst Ehud Eilam told Fox News Digital the exercise is aimed mainly at non-state actors in Syria, Lebanon and Jordan, with or without Iranian backing, and described it as the biggest in recent years. He said it also serves as a message to Iran and others not to provoke Israel on election day. Another expert cited by the outlet invoked the 1973 Yom Kippur War, when Egypt and Syria used exercises to mask preparations for a surprise attack, warning of a possible dangerous miscalculation.

The drills add to a tense regional backdrop that includes earlier-reported U.S. embassy staffing reductions over Iranian threats and escalating Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. Israeli officials have not indicated the exercise targets Iran directly.

stories.headline: Update: More Than 1,300 Arrested as Clashes Follow Second Weekend of Mass Protests in France
stories.summary:
More than 1,300 people were arrested across France on Saturday as hundreds of thousands took part in a second weekend of protests over the cost of living and poor school conditions. The interior ministry estimated 410,000 demonstrators, while unions put the figure near 800,000. Largely peaceful marches were followed by clashes in several cities, with police using tear gas and water cannon.

About 70,000 officers were deployed, and officials avoided the scale of rioting and looting seen on Oct. 17, which produced some of the worst disorder in modern French history. In Paris, 142 people were arrested, less than half the number a week earlier, after a march from Porte d'Italie to Porte de Vincennes ended in clashes. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said several thousand radical activists gathered at the rear of the march, including about 500 identified as rioters. Fifty-three officers were hurt nationwide, and two people were reported seriously injured.

Barricades were set alight in Marseille, boards were stripped from a shop in Bordeaux, and police used tear gas on students in Lyon. President Emmanuel Macron had decreed that only demonstrations organized by recognized trade unions would be permitted, and hundreds have been jailed after fast-track hearings.

Bloomberg reported that Macron won his bet that heavy policing could prevent a repeat of the earlier violence, but has few bargaining chips to resolve the underlying anger, which shows few signs of abating.

stories.headline: Update: Uganda Imposes 21-Day Quarantine on Citizens Returning From DR Congo as Ebola Spreads
stories.summary:
Uganda's health ministry announced Sunday that Ugandans returning from the Democratic Republic of Congo must undergo 21 days of quarantine at their own cost. Travelers who have been in DR Congo will not be allowed to transit through Uganda, and only essential travelers will be admitted under intense public health measures. Screening has been intensified at Entebbe International Airport and all land border crossings.

More than 4,800 people have died in DR Congo since May in the country's deadliest Ebola outbreak, which has spread to several other countries. The measures follow cases in Kenya and Nigeria involving travelers who passed through Entebbe on the same day. Kenya has confirmed eight other cases after a businessman who traveled from DR Congo died two days after arriving in Nairobi, and a related woman died over the weekend.

The patient in Nigeria is the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat who had traveled to Kampala on holiday. Uganda and Nigeria are working to establish her full travel history and routes of exposure. Ugandan officials say no cases have been recorded within the country, which was declared Ebola-free by the WHO in August after 20 cases and two deaths. All 60 contacts of the Kenyan patient have been discharged from monitoring.

Health Minister Chris Baryomunsi said the risk has not ended and urged continued vigilance, given Uganda's border with DR Congo.

stories.headline: Data Center Backlash Grows Worldwide, Becoming a Midterm Election Issue in the US
stories.summary:
Public opposition to data centers is growing around the world as the AI boom drives rapid construction and heavy electricity demand. In the United States, the issue has become prominent ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, with both Republican and Democratic politicians voicing opposition to development in their areas.

There are about 12,250 data centers worldwide, up from roughly 8,000 operational sites in 2021, according to Data Center Map. The US has 4,767 sites and leads by a wide margin in capacity, followed by China, while Europe lags. Larger facilities are increasingly being built in rural areas, and the biggest under construction are dedicated to AI computing, such as xAI's Colossus 2, which will house hundreds of thousands of Nvidia chips.

Critics cite strain on local power and water resources and environmental effects. Activists say the 41 methane gas turbines planned for Colossus 2 could significantly increase local air pollution, while local regulators say the turbines will meet air quality standards.

The backlash puts opponents at odds with President Donald Trump, who has dismissed the pushback as a "sick conspiracy," even as public anger grows. Supporters of expansion argue the facilities bring economic benefits and are essential to staying competitive in AI, a concern raised particularly in Europe.
